speakers: Tobias J. Moskowitz (University of Chicago Booth, NBER, AQR consultant)
Lasse Heje Pedersen (NYU Stern, CBS, AQR, CEPR, NBER)
summary: Question: do value and momentum premia exist across eight markets/asset classes (US, UK, Europe, Japan stocks; country indices; currencies; bonds; commodities), how are they correlated, and what explains the common structure? Method: simple uniform value and 2-12 month momentum signals, tercile portfolios and rank-weighted long-short factors, 1972-2011, with factor, PCA, liquidity-risk, Fama-MacBeth and GRS tests. Conclusion: premia are positive everywhere, value-with-value and momentum-with-momentum correlations are positive across assets while value-momentum is negative, the 50/50 combination reaches Sharpe about 1.4-1.6, and funding liquidity risk (mainly post-1998) explains only part of it; a global three-factor model prices 48 test assets, Fama-French portfolios and hedge funds.

reasoning.question: Are value and momentum premia a U.S.-stock curiosity or a pervasive feature of all liquid markets, do they share common sources across asset classes, and what single parsimonious model could describe global multi-asset returns? For an investor this decides whether value and momentum can be diversified across asset classes, whether a value+momentum combination is a robust core allocation, and what risks (e.g., funding liquidity) the positions carry.

thesis.statement: Value and momentum earn positive premia in every major asset class, value co-moves with value and momentum with momentum across unrelated markets while the two are negatively correlated, and a global market+value+momentum model prices these portfolios, U.S. stock portfolios and hedge funds better than U.S. factors; funding liquidity risk explains part of the comovement (especially after 1998) but not the premia, and the 50/50 combination remains a large, liquidity-neutral puzzle.

reasoning.forward_looking_inputs: (reader) Cross-sectional ranks of (a) multi-year cheapness - negative 5-year price/real exchange-rate change, 5-year rise in 10y yields or (better) real yield and term spread for bonds, BE/ME for stocks and country indices - and (b) 12-1 month relative returns are the inputs that lead returns over the next month (rebalanced monthly; effect horizon roughly months to a few years). They work through slow-moving capital/return chasing (momentum) and later overshoot correction (value), with risk compensation and funding constraints in the background. Funding liquidity shocks (TED, LIBOR-repo, swap-T-bill spreads; AR(2) residuals) are contemporaneous drivers, not predictors: worsening funding hurts momentum and helps value. What would make them stop working: arbitrage capital crowding raising correlations (seen post-1998), sharp liquidity rebounds that crash momentum (2009), and for value long bubbles (1999-2000); the 50/50 mix is the version least exposed to these regime swings.
reader_inferences: (reader) The combo factor column in Table I appears rescaled (not a literal 0.5/0.5 average) for several asset classes; scaling not stated.

(reader) Table VII post-1998 conditional Sharpe ratios look arithmetically inconsistent with the unconditional post-1998 row, and Table VII Sharpe levels match the P3-P1 tercile spreads rather than the rank factors.
(reader) Large value drawdowns around 1999-2000 and a momentum drop around 2009 are visible in Figure 2 but not discussed in the text.
(reader) Bond value (baseline measure) does not share the common factor (PC1 loading ~0) and has a deep 1980s-early 1990s drawdown, so bond results are fragile.
(reader) Funding-liquidity regressions use contemporaneous shocks; they describe risk exposure, not a timing signal.
(reader) Ex post volatility weights and full-sample normalisation mean the published Sharpe ratios are not exactly implementable; costs would lower stock strategies most.

(reader) Part of the three-factor model's pricing success on the 48 portfolios is mechanical because VAL/MOM factors are built from the same securities (equation 5), which the authors acknowledge; the leave-one-out equation (4) R2 of 0.55 is the cleaner evidence.
